examples: Worked mini-analysis (original, illustrative): Lambda Bank finances coal projects while publishing a glossy 'green banking' report; staff turnover is 35% with no grievance mechanism; the board has 9 members, 1 independent, and the CEO chairs the audit committee. Classification table: Environmental — coal financing (negative; financed emissions), glossy report vs reality (greenwashing risk). Social — 35% turnover, no grievance channel (negative; talent and conduct risk). Governance — 1/9 independent directors, CEO chairing audit committee (negative; weak oversight). Inter-connection: weak governance (no independent challenge) ENABLES the environmental misstatement and the social neglect — one line linking the pillars earns the D.2 mark. Greenwashing verdict: the 'green banking' claim is misleading — environmental evidence contradicts it, and S/G are undisclosed. Recommendations aligned with a recognized framework: (1) adopt ISSB IFRS S2-style climate disclosures — financed-emissions inventory with targets; (2) social: grievance mechanism + turnover-reduction target, reported under GRI-style labour indicators; (3) governance: majority-independent board, independent audit-committee chair; (4) independent assurance over the sustainability disclosures. Each recommendation names its pillar — mirroring the classification the examiner asked for.
misconceptions: 1) Unclassified lists — the costliest D error; always label E/S/G. 2) Environment-only greenwashing analysis. 3) Pillars treated as silos — inter-connection is a named LO (D.2). 4) 'Sustainability = philanthropy' — governance and economic viability are pillars too. 5) Recommending 'be more sustainable' without framework, targets, or assurance. 6) Inventing computations — D has no numerical LOs; don't force ratios into it. 7) Citing frameworks you can't describe — if you name GRI or ISSB S1/S2, add one line on what each covers. 8) Assuming pre-2025 questions exist for D — they don't; the only history is Spring 2026 (and Autumn 2026 papers, whose examiner comments are not yet published).
examiner_expectations: All D evidence is Spring 2026 (n=3 of 221 observations; only 7 mapped questions; 32 mapped marks): 'Candidates listed sustainability matters from the scenario but did not classify each under the Environmental, Social or Governance pillar as required — identification alone earned no marks' (BIA-OBS-2026S-005). 'Although the greenwashing conclusion was usually right, justifications covered only environmental failures and ignored social and governance ones' (BIA-OBS-2026S-006). 'Candidates saw why sustainability mattered to the case company but could not recommend actions to align the company with a recognized sustainability framework' (BIA-OBS-2026S-007). So the D answer has three scored moves: classify, justify-across-pillars, recommend-with-framework. Because the area is new and tested at P1/T1, expect discuss/explain requirements (8-12 marks) rather than long cases; structure and completeness beat sophistication.
quick_notes: D = 10-15%, NEW, all P1/T1. D.1: sustainability definition; stakeholders incl. environment. D.2: E / S / Governance-economic pillars + inter-connection (say it explicitly). D.3: pillar KPIs; ESG in capital allocation; GRI / ISSB S1-S2 as recognized frameworks; greenwashing = claim vs pillar-by-pillar evidence. Protocol: harvest → classify table (E/S/G, +/-) → inter-connection line → greenwashing verdict → framework-aligned recommendations → one-line business case. Traps: unclassified lists; environment-only justifications; siloed pillars; generic recommendations. Evidence: 3 Spring 2026 obs, 7 mapped questions — study-text-first topic.

title: Introduction to Sustainability — mastery and exam technique
overview: Mastery-level own-teaching notes for grid area D. Trains materiality-based prioritization, the governance-as-root-cause lens, credibility mechanics (specific/measurable/assured claims), trade-off acknowledgment, and tight timed answers for P1/T1 requirements. D is 10-15% of the paper and the most predictable new area — a scoring opportunity for the prepared. All examples original.
key_concepts: **Evaluation in D:** prioritize by materiality — not all pillars matter equally to every business; a water-intensive dyer is judged on water first. Name the trade-off: sustainability investment has short-term cost and long-term licence-to-operate value; examiners credit balanced judgment over cheerleading. **Credibility mechanics:** specific, measurable, assured claims beat adjectives — 'reduced water intensity 30% by 2028, assured' vs 'eco-friendly'. This is the anti-greenwashing toolkit and doubles as your recommendation template. **Governance as root cause:** in most scenario cases, environmental/social failures trace to governance gaps (no oversight, no targets, no assurance) — making governance the highest-leverage recommendation. **D's place in the paper:** 10-15 marks, likely one Section A question — a reliable, low-variance scoring opportunity if you master the classification discipline; don't leave these marks to chance by under-preparing the new area.
frameworks: Three pillars + inter-connection + stakeholder map + ESG measures + GRI/ISSB S1-S2 awareness + greenwashing claim-vs-evidence test + materiality (prioritising what matters most — the evaluation move in D answers).
methods: **Timed protocol (10-mark D question, ~18 min):** 0-3: harvest facts; decide the requirement type. 3-6: build the classification table (the skeleton of your answer). 6-14: write — definitions in own words, table, inter-connection paragraph, verdict/recommendations. 14-18: check — every fact classified? all three pillars addressed? framework named? trade-off acknowledged? **Verdict template (greenwashing):** 'The claim of [X] is [misleading/partially justified] because [pillar-by-pillar evidence]; the strongest contradiction is [one line]; the company should [framework-aligned action].' **Recommendation template:** '[Pillar]: [specific action] with [target], disclosed under [framework element] and independently assured — addressing [scenario fact].'
examples: Integrated practice case (original, illustrative): Mu Textiles — water-intensive dyeing in a water-stressed region (E: negative, material), 70% female workforce with equal-pay certification (S: positive), zero lost-time injuries for 3 years (S: positive), family-dominated board with no sustainability committee (G: negative), marketing claims '100% sustainable fashion' (greenwashing test). Verdict: the claim is misleading — one strong social record does not offset material environmental harm and weak governance; '100%' language with a water-stressed dyeing operation fails the environmental pillar outright. Inter-connection: weak governance (no sustainability committee) explains why the environmental risk was never managed and why marketing overclaimed — governance is the root cause. Recommendations: (1) E: water-recycling plant + effluent targets disclosed under an ISSB S2-style water/climate disclosure; (2) S: extend the equal-pay audit across the supply chain (GRI-style labour disclosures); (3) G: board sustainability committee with an independent chair; marketing claims rewritten to specific, verifiable statements; (4) independent assurance on the sustainability report. Trade-off acknowledged: the recycling plant costs Rs 120m — fund from the energy savings and position it as licence-to-operate protection, not just cost. Evaluation line: Mu's social strength is real but immaterial to its biggest risk (water) — prioritise by materiality, a recognized-framework concept worth naming.
misconceptions: Mastery traps: 1) Overwriting D — P1/T1 means concise, complete answers; length doesn't add marks. 2) Ignoring materiality — treating a minor positive as offsetting a major negative. 3) Cheerleading ('sustainability is always win-win') instead of acknowledging cost and trade-offs. 4) Forgetting governance — the root-cause pillar in most cases. 5) Waiting for more past papers before studying D — the study text plus the 3 Spring 2026 observations are enough; the examiner tests LOs plainly in new areas.
examiner_expectations: D mastery is about completeness and credibility under thin evidence: with only 2 sessions of history, the examiner will test the LOs plainly — expect 'explain', 'discuss', 'identify and classify', 'evaluate the claim' requirements. Strong answers: own-words definitions, exhaustive classification, explicit inter-connection, framework-named recommendations, and honest handling of trade-offs (e.g., sustainability investment vs short-term cost). Because D is P1/T1, don't overwrite — a tight, fully-classified 10-mark answer beats a sprawling one. Watch Autumn 2026 examiner comments when published; they will double the evidence base.
quick_notes: Mastery D = classify completely + prioritize by materiality + name trade-offs. Governance is usually the root cause — recommend there first. Anti-greenwashing toolkit: specific, measurable, assured claims. Timed: 3 min harvest/table, 8 min write, 4 min check. Templates: verdict (claim → pillar evidence → contradiction → action); recommendation (pillar: action + target + framework + assurance). P1/T1: tight beats long. Evidence still thin — watch for Autumn 2026 examiner comments; until then, study-text-first.

title: Knowledge Reference - quick revision
overview: The Specific Examinable Knowledge Reference (topic KR, no weightage of its own) lists 13 named models and techniques examiners may require you to USE: strategy models (SWOT, Porter, PLC, BCG), ethics models (Tucker, AAA), ISO 31000, CAPM, the NEW capital rationing and asset replacement cycle, and hedging instruments for interest rates, FX, and commodities. They are tested as tools inside scenario questions across areas A, B and C - never as standalone theory essays. Own teaching notes - paraphrased, not ICAP text.
key_concepts: **Strategy models (KR1-KR4):** SWOT (internal/external split), Porter (five forces), PLC (intro/growth/maturity/decline), BCG (star/cash cow/question mark/dog on growth vs relative share). **Ethics models (KR5-KR6):** Tucker five questions (structured probing: legality, fairness, relationships, consequences, conscience); AAA seven steps (facts, issue, stakeholders/norms, alternatives, evaluate, decide, monitor). **Risk model (KR7):** ISO 31000 process - context, identification, analysis, evaluation, treatment, monitoring and review. **Finance model (KR8):** CAPM - Ke = Rf + beta x (Rm - Rf). **New (KR9-KR10):** capital rationing (profitability-index ranking; combinations for indivisible projects; hard vs soft rationing); asset replacement cycle (equivalent annual cost/benefit for different lives). **Hedging (KR11-KR13):** interest-rate futures/options/forwards; FX futures/options/forwards/money-market hedge; commodity and security forwards/futures. Options = right not obligation (premium); futures = standardized exchange contracts (whole contracts, ticks); forwards = customized OTC.
frameworks: KR1 SWOT. KR2 Porter's Five Forces. KR3 Product Life Cycle. KR4 BCG Matrix. KR5 Tucker five-question model. KR6 AAA seven-step model. KR7 ISO 31000 risk-management guidelines. KR8 CAPM. KR9 Capital rationing. KR10 Asset replacement cycle. KR11 Interest-rate hedging (futures, options, forwards). KR12 FX hedging (currency futures, options, forwards, money-market hedge). KR13 Commodity and security forwards/futures. Hedge-efficiency measurement excluded throughout.
methods: Model-application routine (same for all 13): (1) Name the model and state its purpose in one line. (2) Feed it the scenario's facts - models are empty without inputs. (3) Read off the model's output (quadrant, force assessment, decision, hedge). (4) Translate the output into the requirement's answer (recommendation, evaluation, classification). Never describe a model at length without applying it - examiners mark the application. For ethics models, end with an explicit decision. For hedging, end with the named instrument and why.
examples: Original one-line applications (illustrative): KR1 - a snack company's strong brand (S) vs rising sugar taxes (T). KR2 - five-forces on a ride-hailing entrant facing driver bargaining power. KR3 - a smartphone model in maturity: defend share, cut cost. KR4 - two product lines: one star, one dog, using the scenario's 10% growth cut-off. KR5/KR6 - trainee asked to backdate documents: run the five questions / seven steps, decide, escalate. KR7 - a bank's risk register: context, identify, analyze, evaluate, treat, monitor. KR8 - beta 1.3, Rf 9%, Rm 15% gives Ke = 16.8%. KR9 - Rs 100m budget, indivisible projects: test affordable combinations, max combined NPV wins. KR10 - machine lives 3 vs 5 years: compare equivalent annual cost. KR11 - floating-rate loan: buy an interest-rate cap (option) to limit upside while keeping downside. KR12 - USD payable in 90 days, firm: buy USD forward. KR13 - wheat miller: buy wheat futures to lock input cost.
misconceptions: 1) Describing models instead of using them - the classic KR mark-loss. 2) BCG without the scenario's cut-offs. 3) CAPM beta as total risk. 4) Forward vs futures confusion (OTC customized vs exchange standardized). 5) Options treated as free - the premium is part of the cost. 6) Hedge efficiency - excluded; don't compute it. 7) Ethics: reciting all principles instead of selecting. 8) KR9/KR10 assumed to be 'just NPV' - they are distinct methods (ranking/annuity logic).
examiner_expectations: No examiner observations are tagged directly to KR (0 of 221) - but the models appear constantly inside area A/B/C questions, so their examiner expectations live there: BCG - use the scenario's cut-offs; criticize as applied, not generically (BIA-OBS-2022S-004/006); ethics models - select relevant principles, don't list everything (BIA-OBS-2022S-008/009); CAPM - state the formula and inputs (BIA-OBS-2022S-016); hedging - rate and contract mechanics decide marks (BIA-OBS-2022A-020/022/023/024). Examiners test KR items as TOOLS inside scenario questions, not as standalone theory - know each model's purpose, inputs, and output in one line. New KR9 (capital rationing) and KR10 (asset replacement cycle) have no past-paper history - learn the method from the study text.
quick_notes:
KR = 13 tools, tested inside A/B/C scenarios. KR1-4 strategy (SWOT, Porter, PLC, BCG); KR5-6 ethics (Tucker, AAA); KR7 ISO 31000 process; KR8 CAPM; KR9 NEW capital rationing (PI ranking/combinations); KR10 NEW asset replacement (equivalent annual cost); KR11-13 hedging (futures/options/forwards; money-market for FX). Rules: name, feed scenario facts, read output, answer the requirement. Traps: BCG cut-offs; beta = systematic; forwards OTC vs futures exchange; premium counts; no hedge-efficiency; select ethics principles. 0 direct observations - evidence lives in the area notes.

Self-test: (1) Requirement asks for 'competitive position of the division' - which KR tool, and what are its five components? (2) Two machines with lives 3 and 5 years: which KR method compares them, and what is its formula? (3) Futures vs forwards vs options: state one difference on each of standardization, obligation, and cost.

title: Knowledge Reference - detailed study notes
overview: Detailed own-teaching notes for the 13 Specific Examinable Knowledge References: purpose, inputs, mechanics, output, and one evaluation-ready limitation for each of KR1-KR13, with requirement-matching guidance and worked original applications. KR items are examined as tools inside scenario questions - these notes train tool selection and application, not memorization. All content paraphrased own-teaching.
key_concepts: **KR1 SWOT:** 2x2 of internal (strengths/weaknesses) vs external (opportunities/threats); TOWS thinking - SO, WO, ST, WT strategies. **KR2 Porter:** five forces determine industry attractiveness; analyze each force separately with scenario evidence, then judge overall. **KR3 PLC:** introduction (negative cash flow, skimming/penetration pricing), growth (rising sales, invest in capacity), maturity (peak, defend share, cost focus), decline (harvest or divest); strategy must match the stage. **KR4 BCG:** axes = market growth rate and RELATIVE market share (vs largest competitor); quadrants and standard strategies; use scenario cut-offs. **KR5 Tucker:** five probing questions testing legality, stakeholder fairness, relationship/reputation effects, long-term consequences, and the conscience/publicity test. **KR6 AAA:** seven-step decision process - facts, ethical issue, stakeholders and norms, alternatives, evaluation of alternatives, decision, monitoring. **KR7 ISO 31000:** principles plus the risk-management process (scope/context, risk assessment [identify, analyze, evaluate], treatment, monitoring/review, communication). **KR8 CAPM:** Ke = Rf + beta x (Rm - Rf); beta = systematic-risk sensitivity; SML; assumptions and limits. **KR9 Capital rationing:** hard (market won't fund) vs soft (management caps); divisible, profitability index ranking; indivisible, combinations; multi-period, programming methods (concept only). **KR10 Asset replacement:** equivalent annual cost = PV of all costs divided by annuity factor; equivalent annual benefit for revenue-generating comparisons; assumes like-for-like replacement continues. **KR11 Interest-rate hedging:** futures (lock a rate; standardized), options - caps/floors/collars (premium for protection with retained benefit), forward rate agreements (customized lock; OTC). **KR12 FX hedging:** currency futures, currency options, forward contracts, money-market hedge (borrow/deposit across currencies); match the tool to certainty of exposure. **KR13 Commodity and security:** forward and future contracts to lock input/output prices; same mechanics as KR11/12 applied to commodities.
frameworks: Full KR1-KR13 set as in the quick notes, each with: purpose, inputs, mechanics, output, one limitation. Limitations bank: SWOT - static snapshot, no prioritization; Porter - defines industry narrowly, underplays dynamics; PLC - stages hard to identify in real time; BCG - only two dimensions, ignores synergies; Tucker/AAA - judgment still required, models don't decide; ISO 31000 - only as good as the risk culture; CAPM - assumptions (single period, efficient markets, stable beta); rationing PI - assumes divisibility for ranking; EAC - assumes repeatable replacement; hedging - basis risk, cost, margin.
methods: **Requirement-matching (which tool?):** 'competitive position/industry' goes to Porter; 'product mix/portfolio' to BCG/PLC; 'internal vs external picture' to SWOT; 'right thing to do' to Tucker/AAA; 'risk process/register' to ISO 31000; 'required return/cost of equity' to CAPM; 'limited budget, choose projects' to KR9; 'replace machine, different lives' to KR10; 'interest-rate exposure' to KR11; 'currency exposure' to KR12; 'commodity price exposure' to KR13. **Application write-up per model:** one line of purpose, scenario facts as inputs, model's output stated plainly, implication for the requirement, one limitation (evaluation mark). **Hedging selection:** certain exposure goes to forward/future/money-market (compare cost); uncertain goes to option; always state the residual (basis risk/premium).
examples: Detailed applications (original, illustrative): (1) BCG - scenario gives market growth 12% vs cut-off 10%, relative shares 1.4 and 0.3: product X (high growth, share 1.4) = star, invest; product Y (growth 4%, share 0.3) = dog, harvest; the cut-off came from the scenario, not memory. (2) Porter - cement industry: new entrants blocked by capital intensity (low threat); suppliers (coal/energy) concentrated (high power); buyers (dealers) fragmented (low power); substitutes low short-term; rivalry high among 4 large players - attractiveness moderate, advantage from cost leadership. (3) Tucker/AAA - procurement manager offered a kickback: facts (offer, amount, timing); issue (integrity vs personal gain); stakeholders (employer, supplier, self, profession); principles (integrity, objectivity, professional behaviour); options (accept/refuse/report); decision: refuse and report - integrity is absolute, concealment compounds the breach. (4) ISO 31000 - IT outage risk at a bank: context (24/7 service obligation); identify (server failure); analyze (likelihood x impact); evaluate (against tolerance); treat (redundant systems = reduce; insurance = transfer); monitor (uptime KPIs). (5) CAPM - project beta 1.25, Rf 10%, Rm 16% gives required return 17.5%; use as the discount rate. (6) Rationing - budget 150; projects A(90, NPV 27), B(70, NPV 21), C(60, NPV 18), D(40, NPV 10); indivisible combos: A+C=150 NPV 45 (best); A+D=130 NPV 37; B+C=130 NPV 39; B+D=110 NPV 31; C+D=100 NPV 28 - choose A+C. (7) Replacement - press P: cost 200, life 4, PV of operating costs 180, total PV 380, annuity factor (10%,4y) 3.1699, EAC 119.9; press Q: cost 280, life 6, PV operating 240, total 520, factor 4.3553, EAC 119.4 - Q marginally cheaper per year. (8) FX hedge - importer owes USD 500k in 6 months (firm): forward at 282 vs money-market via borrow-invest; pick the cheaper certain cost; if the order were contingent on a contract win, buy a USD call option instead.
misconceptions: 1) Using the wrong model for the requirement - match first, apply second. 2) BCG/Porter/SWOT written generically with no scenario facts. 3) Ethics models used as decoration (described, then ignored in the decision). 4) ISO 31000 recited as principles when the question asked for the PROCESS on a scenario risk. 5) CAPM applied to total risk or with book-value inputs. 6) Rationing by NPV rank for indivisible projects. 7) EAC compared across options without matching cost-vs-benefit framing. 8) Futures/forwards/options confused on standardization, obligation, and cost. 9) Hedge efficiency computed - excluded from the syllabus. 10) Assuming KR items are 'theory questions' - they are tools; the theory-only answer scores poorly.
examiner_expectations: KR items are examined through application: the BCG observations (use given cut-offs; apply criticism to the scenario - BIA-OBS-2022S-004/006), ethics observations (select relevant principles - BIA-OBS-2022S-008/009), CAPM (show formula and inputs - BIA-OBS-2022S-016), and hedging mechanics (rates, rounding, ticks - BIA-OBS-2022A-020/022/023/024) are all KR tools being tested inside area questions. Detailed expectation: for each model, know (a) when it is the RIGHT tool (requirement-matching), (b) its inputs and mechanics, (c) its output format, and (d) one limitation for evaluation marks. New KR9/KR10: show full method - examiners calibrate new topics on visible working.
quick_notes: KR detailed = 13 tools, each: purpose, inputs, mechanics, output, 1 limitation. Match the requirement first (industry to Porter, portfolio to BCG/PLC, ethics to Tucker/AAA, risk process to ISO 31000, return to CAPM, budget limit to KR9, replacement to KR10, rate/FX/commodity exposure to KR11/12/13). Apply with scenario facts; end models with decisions, hedging with the named instrument + reason. Limitations bank ready for evaluation marks. New KR9/KR10: full visible method. Never describe without applying; never compute hedge efficiency.

title: Knowledge Reference - mastery and exam technique
overview: Mastery-level own-teaching notes for the Knowledge Reference: tool-switching across KR1-KR13 inside integrated Section B-style cases, synthesis chains (strategy to finance to risk to ethics), tool-choice justification, and timed mixed-case protocol. The KR list is a toolbox, not a syllabus chapter - mastery is reaching for the right tool without being told. All examples original.
key_concepts: **Synthesis:** the KR tools form a decision chain - strategy tools (KR1-KR4) set direction, finance tools (KR8-KR10) test affordability, risk tools (KR7, KR11-KR13) protect the plan, ethics tools (KR5-KR6) guard its integrity. In answers, make the chain visible: 'The BCG analysis (dog to harvest) frees Rs Xm, which the NPV appraisal (KR9 rationing) allocates to the star product; the FX exposure on imported inputs is hedged with forwards (KR12).' **Tool-choice justification:** one line per tool on WHY it fits the requirement - examiners credit this explicitly in new-topic areas. **Speed:** know each model's output format cold (quadrant name, force verdict, hedge name, decision) so application, not recall, consumes your time.
frameworks: All KR1-KR13 deployed in combination; mastery is tool-switching and synthesis, not deeper theory.
methods: **Timed protocol (15-mark mixed case):** 0-4 min: split the requirement into sub-tasks; assign one tool per sub-task; harvest facts per tool. 4-16: apply each tool compactly - purpose line, facts, output, implication. 16-24: synthesis paragraph + recommendations; ethics decision stated. 24-27: check - every sub-requirement answered? tool choices justified? limitations noted (1-2)? new-topic methods fully shown? **Synthesis template:** '[Tool A] shows [output]; therefore [Tool B] is applied to [decision], giving [result]; the residual [risk] is handled with [Tool C]; the ethical dimension is [decision]. Overall recommendation: [one sentence].'
examples: Integrated practice case (original, illustrative): Sigma Appliances - portfolio: air conditioners (star: high growth, share leader), fans (cash cow), heaters (dog). Requirement set: (a) analyze the competitive position of the AC division (Porter: supplier power high - compressor imports; buyer power moderate; new entrants low - brand/capital barriers; substitutes low; rivalry intense on price; position strong on brand, squeezed on cost); (b) evaluate the portfolio (BCG with scenario cut-offs: milk the fans to fund the AC star; harvest heaters); (c) the AC expansion needs Rs 200m - appraise via NPV at the divisional hurdle rate (CAPM-derived), under a soft capital rationing cap that also covers the fan-line upgrade (KR9: indivisible, combinations); the old stamping press (4 years left) vs a new one (7 years) - KR10 equivalent annual cost; (d) imported compressors create USD exposure - forward cover for firm orders, options for tender-contingent volumes (KR12); (e) the sales head proposes understating warranty provisions to 'support the share price' - Tucker/AAA: integrity breach, refuse and escalate (KR5/KR6). Synthesis: fund AC expansion (star, positive NPV), ration in favour of it over the fan upgrade, hedge the compressor exposure, and hold the ethics line - one paragraph tying all five tools to a single recommendation. This is what a 15-mark Section B answer looks like: five tools, one story.
misconceptions: Mastery traps: 1) Applying every tool you know instead of the ones the requirement needs. 2) Perfect single-tool answers with no synthesis - Section B rewards the joined-up story. 3) Ethics bolted on as an afterthought - integrate it where the scenario plants it. 4) New tools (KR9/KR10) either avoided or over-explained - apply normally, show method. 5) Forgetting that KR tools serve areas A/B/C answers - the topic page is a reference; the exam is integrated.
examiner_expectations: KR mastery = fluent tool-switching inside mixed questions: a Section B case can require Porter (A.a.4) + BCG (A.b.1) + NPV (C.3) + a hedge recommendation (B.4) in one requirement set. Examiners reward candidates who pick the right tool per sub-requirement without being told, apply each cleanly, and synthesize - e.g., the portfolio decision (BCG) driving the investment appraisal (NPV) driving the funding/hedging choice. With KR9/KR10 new and KR evidence indirect, visible method and explicit tool-choice reasoning ('Porter is appropriate here because the requirement asks about competitive position') earn the benefit of the doubt.
quick_notes: Mastery KR = right tool, clean application, visible synthesis. Chain: strategy tools set direction, finance tools test affordability, risk tools protect, ethics tools guard integrity. Protocol: split requirement, one tool per sub-task, apply compactly, synthesis paragraph, check. Template: [Tool A output] to [Tool B decision] to [Tool C residual risk] to ethics decision to one-sentence recommendation. Justify each tool choice in one line. New KR9/KR10: apply normally, full method shown. Never tool-dump; never skip synthesis.
